turns.originalText: Let me give you the TTS-optimized explanatory version first, then the tables. --- The fundamental unit you need to understand is torque, measured in Newton-meters. Think of it this way: if you have a wrench that's one meter long and you push on the end with ten Newtons of force, you're applying ten Newton-meters of torque to whatever you're turning. A motor rated at thirty Newton-meters can hold that same force at that same distance. Now here's where it gets practical: your arm is about 0.4 meters from shoulder to hand. To hold a seven kilogram weight at full extension, gravity pulls down with about seventy Newtons. Multiply by 0.4 meters and you need twenty-eight Newton-meters just to hold it still. To actually lift it, to accelerate it upward, you need more. How much more depends on how fast you want to move. If you want to move that seven kilos through a half meter arc in one second, you're accelerating at roughly two meters per second squared, which adds another fourteen Newtons of force requirement. So now you need maybe thirty-five Newton-meters total. This is why robot arms doing dynamic lifting need motors rated at one and a half to two times the static holding requirement. The difference between hobby servos and industrial servos comes down to a few key things. Hobby servos like the Dynamixel XM series use plastic or metal gears, have maybe thirty Newton-meters peak torque, cost a few hundred dollars, and wear out after a few thousand hours of heavy use. Industrial servos from Kollmorgen or Maxon use frameless designs where the motor integrates directly into the joint, have harmonic drives or cycloidal reducers that handle a hundred plus Newton-meters with near-zero backlash, cost thousands of dollars per joint, and run for tens of thousands of hours. The real difference is in the reducer. A harmonic drive has a flexible spline that engages with a wave generator, giving you gear ratios of fifty to one or higher with backlash under one arc-minute. That precision is what lets industrial robots hit repeatability of plus or minus fifty microns instead of plus or minus one millimeter. Current control versus PWM is about precision and smoothness. PWM tells the motor to be on for some percentage of each cycle, which works fine for position holding but creates torque ripple during motion. Current control directly regulates the electromagnetic field, giving you smooth torque output that's proportional to your command signal. This matters for force-sensitive tasks. If you're trying to apply exactly five Newtons of force while the arm contacts a surface, PWM will give you choppy oscillating force while current control gives you steady pressure. Industrial robots doing polishing, grinding, or assembly absolutely need current control. Your tabletop arm doing pick and place can get away with PWM. The hierarchical architecture you're building in your head is sound but the timing relationships need refinement. The narrator LLM doesn't need to run constantly. It fires when the user gives a new command or when the robot completes a task and needs to know what's next. Call it once every five to thirty seconds during active operation. Its output is a structured intent like "pick up the red block from position A and place it in the left bin" which persists until the task is done or something changes. The trajectory VLA runs more frequently because it needs to adapt to what it sees. The scene changes as the robot moves, objects shift, lighting varies. Running at ten to thirty Hertz means it updates its plan every thirty to hundred milliseconds. But here's the key insight: it doesn't plan the entire task every cycle. It outputs a trajectory embedding that represents the next one to two seconds of motion. That embedding captures not just where to go but how to get there, the velocity profile, the grasp approach angle, the expected contact timing. The motor group policies decode that embedding into actual joint trajectories. This is where your octopus intuition is right. Each limb policy can be trained separately on that limb's dynamics. The shoulder joint has different inertia than the wrist. The left arm might have slightly different friction characteristics than the right arm. By having separate small networks, maybe ten million parameters each, you can fine-tune per limb without retraining the whole system. These run at thirty to a hundred Hertz, outputting the next ten to fifty joint position targets. The PID layer at the bottom runs fastest, one to ten kilohertz, and it's not neural at all. It's classical control math. You have a target position from the motor group policy, you have a measured position from the encoder, the PID calculates the error and outputs a current command to minimize that error. This is where microcontrollers like the ESP32 or STM32 live. They handle the fast loop that keeps the motor tracking the trajectory. The feedback question is critical. Does information flow back up the hierarchy? Yes, but at different rates. The PID level feeds back immediately through the encoder. The motor group level gets proprioceptive feedback, the joint positions and velocities, at the same rate it outputs commands. The VLA level gets visual feedback at camera frame rate, thirty to sixty Hertz. The narrator level gets feedback through the VLA's state representation, essentially summarizing "task in progress" or "task complete" or "unexpected obstacle." The time dimension in the matrix multiplication isn't a separate axis in the sense you might be thinking. Each inference is a snapshot. The network sees current image, current joint state, current intent, and outputs next action chunk. The temporal structure is encoded in the sequence of chunks, each one picking up where the last left off. Some architectures like transformers explicitly attend over previous timesteps, keeping a sliding window of recent observations. But the actual matrix multiply is still spatial at any given moment. Spiders as your embodied AI familiar is actually a solid choice for learning. Six or eight legs gives you redundancy, you can lose a leg and keep moving. The gait control problem is well-studied. And there's real research on hexapod and octopod robots that you can build on. Check out the PhantomX hexapod platform or the open-source designs from Trossen Robotics. A spider doesn't need to balance like a biped, which removes a huge chunk of the control problem. It can focus purely on locomotion and manipulation if you add front leg dexterity. The failure modes in current embodied AI cluster around a few things. Distribution shift kills generalization. The robot sees a slightly different background, slightly different lighting, object rotated five degrees from anything in training, and the policy outputs nonsense. Contact transitions are fragile. The moment the gripper touches the object, the dynamics change discontinuously, and policies trained mostly on free-space motion struggle. Long-horizon planning breaks down because small errors compound over many steps. And multimodal integration is still immature. The vision encoder and language encoder were trained separately on different data, their embedding spaces don't align perfectly, so the VLA has to learn that alignment from limited robot data. --- Now the tables: Five tables: servo comparison with prices and payloads, hierarchy timing showing frequencies and latencies, neural net sizing showing what runs where at what speed, budget tiers showing what you can actually build, and failure modes showing where current AI breaks. The closed-loop feedback thing you asked about: it means the system constantly checks reality against expectation. Camera shows gripper drifting left, policy outputs correction to drift right. That's the "loop" being "closed" between sensing and acting. Open-loop would be: execute the plan blindly and hope it works. Closed-loop is why you can build imprecise hardware and still get precise results. For research prompts to spin off, here are three good ones: Research 1: "Current state of hierarchical imitation learning for robot manipulation. What architectures have proven successful? Compare flat end-to-end VLA approaches versus hierarchical options frameworks. Include specific papers from Berkeley, Stanford, and Google DeepMind from 2023-2025. Focus on manipulation not locomotion." Research 2: "Hexapod and spider robot platforms for embodied AI research. What open source designs exist? Compare PhantomX, custom builds, and research platforms. What control approaches work best for multi-legged locomotion with manipulation? Include cost estimates and build complexity." Research 3: "Force and torque sensing integration with learned robot policies. How do researchers incorporate tactile feedback into VLA-style models? What sensors are used, what's the latency, and how does it improve contact-rich manipulation? Focus on practical implementations not just theory." Pick any of those if you want deeper dives.

turns.originalText: Not a dumb idea. The hierarchical neural net pipeline is exactly where embodied AI research is heading. Your intuition about per-motor learned controllers, motor group coordination, and semantic trajectory planning is sound architecture. The question is whether anyone has proven it works better than flat end-to-end, and what the practical tradeoffs are. Let me address the direct questions first, then I'll build you the proper visualization. Breaking down a box and removing tape: Current systems cannot do this reliably. Here's why: the tape has unknown adhesion strength, the cardboard has unknown stiffness, the motion requires force feedback that changes dynamically as the tape peels, and the robot needs to detect when the tape ends. This is exactly the contact-rich manipulation problem that kills current VLAs. Someone could probably get 60-70% success rate with extensive training on that specific box type, but generalized "open any box" is years away. PID replacement with neural nets: Yes, people are doing this. It's called neural network-based motor control or learned dynamics models. The idea is exactly what you're describing: instead of hand-tuned PID gains, train a small network on the specific motor's input-output history. It can learn the nonlinearities, the friction curves, the thermal drift. Google's work on learned motor models for their robots does this. The challenge is training data collection and the risk of instability if the network outputs something unexpected. The hierarchy training question: This is the hard problem. If you train end-to-end, the gradients flow through all layers and everything adapts together. If you train hierarchically with separate networks, you need to define the interfaces between levels, and those interfaces become bottlenecks. The motion capture feedback idea you mentioned, where haptic feedback helps the human demonstrator feel what the robot feels, is called bilateral teleoperation and yes people are doing it. It produces better demonstrations because the human adapts their motion to the actual forces. Your timing intuition: Running the whole pipeline every second with 100 motor commands per second is reasonable. The VLA outputs a trajectory plan, the motor groups decode it into joint targets, the motor-level controllers execute. The two-second subgoal window works. The question is whether you need neural nets at every level or if the motor level can stay classical PID and only go neural for adaptation over longer timescales. turns.originalText: Let me address your questions directly and honestly. VLM as narrator: The VLM (Vision-Language Model) handles both vision AND language, so it's doing scene understanding plus intent parsing in one model. Figure's Helix uses a 7B VLM that looks at cameras and understands "pick up the red cup" simultaneously. The trajectory planner below it is a smaller specialized model that just does vision-to-action, no language reasoning. So yes, two separate concerns: semantic understanding (VLM) and motor planning (visuomotor policy). 80M parameter at 200 Hz: The 80M model outputs joint position targets, not raw motor commands. The motors receive those targets and their internal controllers (or your hybrid neural-PID) execute them. 200 Hz means the policy updates its target 200 times per second, giving very smooth motion. The motors themselves can respond much faster (1-10 kHz internal loops). Helix cost: Figure AI hasn't published pricing, it's not available for purchase. They're deploying it in BMW factories under commercial contracts. Subgoal and action durations - let me be precise here because you asked me to check you: Looking at the actual research: π0.5 predicts subtasks that span 2-10 seconds typically The VLA outputs action chunks of 50-100 timesteps at 10-50 Hz, so roughly 1-2 seconds of motion per inference Motor group policies in Helix output at 200 Hz continuously, not in chunks So the timing is: Narrator fires on task change or completion (variable, could be 5 seconds to 5 minutes). VLA/trajectory runs every 0.5-2 seconds, outputting the next 1-2 seconds of motion. Motor execution is continuous at 100-200 Hz. Why not all running at the same timeframe: Different computational costs. The narrator (8B params) takes 100-500ms to run. The VLA (100-500M params) takes 30-100ms. The motor group (5-50M) takes 5-10ms. The joint controller (100K-1M + PID) takes 0.1-1ms. If you tried to run the narrator at 200 Hz, you'd need impossible compute. The hierarchy exists because different decisions need different amounts of thinking time. Proprioception: Yes, it's the robot's sense of its own body position. Joint angles, velocities, motor currents. Not touch exactly, that's tactile sensing, but internal body awareness. What makes robots slower on the production line: Not the control frequency. It's: Vision processing latency (30-100ms to understand a scene) Conservatism in the policy (trained to be safe, not fast) Settling time (waiting for vibrations to damp before precision moves) Human-imposed speed limits for safety certification Industrial robots CAN move extremely fast. UR5 max speed is 1 m/s, some industrial arms hit 5+ m/s. The limitation is usually the task, not the hardware. Hidden units: Neurons in a layer that isn't input or output. A 2-layer MLP with 32 hidden units means: input layer → 32 neurons → 32 neurons → output layer. Each hidden unit computes a weighted sum of inputs, applies a nonlinearity, passes to the next layer. Zero-shot transfer: The MeMo paper trained a controller on a 6-legged robot. Then they added 2 more legs to the simulation (8 legs total). Without any additional training, the same per-joint policies worked because each joint's controller only sees local information. The network didn't need to "learn" 8 legs because each leg's controller is independent. That's what modular architecture enables. Morphology: Body shape/structure. A spider has different morphology than a humanoid. Morphology transfer means a controller trained on one body shape working on a different body shape. Is the narrator what creates subgoals: Yes, or an intermediate planner layer. The narrator outputs structured intent like "pick up red block, place in bin" which might decompose into subgoals: (1) move to block, (2) grasp, (3) lift, (4) move to bin, (5) release. Some systems do this decomposition explicitly (SayCan, π0.5), others let the VLA figure it out implicitly. Manufacturing box cameras: Yes, one overhead workspace camera plus wrist cameras per arm works. The workspace camera feeds into the shared VLA for scene understanding. Wrist cameras feed into arm-specific policies for close manipulation. This is exactly how ALOHA and similar systems work. Proprioception as VLA input: Correct. The VLA takes camera images AND current joint states AND the narrative/intent. It needs to know where the arm currently is to plan where it should go. Why rerun motor group policy: You're right to question this. Two approaches in practice: Run once per trajectory chunk (every 1-2s), output all 100-200 timesteps, execute open-loop Run continuously at 30-100 Hz, output next 10-50 timesteps, always replanning Approach 2 is more robust because it corrects for disturbances. You're constantly updating your plan based on what actually happened. The "future projection" you mention is implicit, the policy learns to output trajectories that account for expected dynamics. Joint controller anomaly filtering: Separate from output. You monitor motor current and position error. If current spikes unexpectedly (hit something) or position error grows (motor stalling), that's an anomaly signal that propagates up. The joint controller doesn't filter its own output, it reports problems upward. Is this actually happening: Yes. Figure AI is deploying Helix at BMW. Physical Intelligence demonstrated π0 doing laundry folding. These are real systems in real environments. The research I'm citing is from 2024-2025, published and peer-reviewed. This isn't hype, it's the current state of deployed robotics. DAgger-style learning: Dataset Aggregation. The key insight: if you only train on expert demonstrations, the robot never learns to recover from mistakes because the expert never made mistakes. DAgger works like this: Expert demonstrates task, collect data Train policy on expert data Robot executes policy while expert watches When robot deviates, expert corrects (provides the "right" action from that wrong state) Add correction data to training set Retrain, repeat The correction data teaches recovery. Your "operation buzzer" idea is exactly this, except instead of providing the correct action, you're providing a negative signal. That works too, it's called learning from human feedback. The 10-minute training intuition is optimistic but not crazy for simple tasks. Research shows 20-50 demonstrations for basic pick-place with DAgger-style correction. Operation game by year end: Honestly? Possible but aggressive. Operation requires: ~1mm precision (tweezers in narrow slots) Force sensitivity (don't touch the edges) Visual recognition of which piece to grab With good hardware (XM540-class servos, RealSense depth), proper training pipeline, and maybe 100-200 demonstrations with haptic feedback, you could get 70-80% success rate in 6 months of focused work. 95%+ is harder. Spider climbing stairs in 10 seconds: Easier than Operation, ironically. Locomotion is more forgiving than manipulation. Hexapod platforms exist (PhantomX ~$2000). Stair climbing is a solved problem for 6+ legged robots. 10 seconds for a standard staircase is achievable with existing open-source controllers. The MeMo-style modular approach would let you train in simulation and transfer to real hardware. What you should build first: Motion capture rig ($100-150): SlimeVR IMUs on wrist, elbow, shoulder, plus finger tracking for gripper Single arm with teleoperation: SO-101 class ($300-500) with leader-follower or direct IMU mapping Training pipeline: LeRobot or custom, doesn't matter, just get demonstration → policy working Simple task: Pick and place blocks, not Operation. Get the full loop working first. The spider is actually a good parallel project because it's different enough that you're learning two complementary things: manipulation (arm) and locomotion (spider). And the modular architecture research applies to both.

turns.originalText: Let me synthesize what's important from this conversation for you as product owner. Critical architectural clarification you're missing: The reason motor execution runs faster than trajectory planning isn't about "importance" - it's about physics. If your motor only updates its target once per second, and something unexpected happens at 0.1 seconds (object shifts, motor overshoots, external disturbance), you're flying blind for 0.9 seconds. The motor could be forcing against a jammed object, accumulating error, or worse. The 100Hz motor loop isn't doing different computation each time - it's doing error correction. "Am I where I should be? No? Adjust." That happens 100 times per second because physical reality doesn't wait for your trajectory planner to finish thinking. Think of it like steering a car. Your high-level navigation (turn left at the light) updates every few seconds. Your steering corrections (stay in lane, compensate for wind) happen continuously. You don't wait for navigation to recalculate before you correct a drift. The 32x32 parameter question: A 2-layer MLP with 32 hidden units and 6 joint inputs, 6 joint outputs: (6 inputs × 32) + (32 × 32) + (32 × 6 outputs) = 192 + 1024 + 192 = ~1,400 parameters. Add biases, maybe 1,500. That's tiny. A "1 million parameter" motor-level network would have much wider layers or more depth. The research uses small networks because they need to run fast. Bigger doesn't mean better at this level. Approach 1 vs Approach 2 (open-loop vs continuous replanning): Approach 2 (continuous replanning) is strictly better for robustness. The only reason to use Approach 1 is compute constraints - if you can't run inference fast enough. On Jetson hardware with 10-50M parameter models, you can replan continuously. The "instability" concern would be if the replanning introduced jitter (constantly changing targets causing oscillation), but proper trajectory smoothing handles that. LeRobot's role: LeRobot covers: data collection interfaces, policy architectures (ACT, Diffusion Policy), training loops, basic deployment. What it doesn't cover: the hierarchical multi-level architecture you're describing, the narrator/task decomposition layer, per-motor learned controllers, or the glue between levels. You'd use LeRobot for the VLA/trajectory layer training, then build custom integration above and below it. Hardware overlap between Operation and Spider: Shared components: Jetson compute, camera systems, training pipeline, the entire software architecture above the motor group level. Different components: Servos (arm manipulation needs precision, spider locomotion needs speed/torque tradeoff differently), frame (obviously), gripper vs feet. The neural network training methodology transfers. The motion capture rig works for both. Maybe 40% hardware overlap, 80% software/architecture overlap. Quality metrics you should track: Kinematic fidelity: Your motion capture position vs robot actual position, measured in mm RMS error Temporal fidelity: Latency between your motion and robot motion, measured in ms Force transparency (if doing haptic): Robot contact force vs what you feel, measured as ratio Demonstration consistency: Given same task, how similar are repeated demonstrations (variance in trajectories) Policy success rate: After training, what percentage of attempts complete the task The gap between "pick up block" (±5mm tolerance, any orientation) and "play Operation" (±1mm tolerance, specific insertion angle, force-sensitive) is roughly 5x tighter precision requirements. That's achievable with good hardware, but it means your training data also needs to be 5x cleaner. Three things you should decide now: First hardware purchase: Motion capture IMUs ($75-100) to prove you can capture your own movements accurately. This is useful for both arm and spider paths. Compute platform commitment: Jetson Orin Nano ($500) is the floor for real neural policy inference. Stop looking for cheaper alternatives - a phone won't work, a Pi won't work. This is a fixed cost. First robot form factor: I'd recommend single arm over spider for your stated food pantry goal. The spider is seductive but doesn't help you bag groceries. Arm with parallel gripper on a constrained workspace directly addresses your use case. Do you want me to spec the exact BOM and build sequence for a single-arm motion-capture-trained manipulation cell?

turns.originalText: Let me address your pushback directly because you're right to challenge me. Motor execution frequency - you caught something: You're correct that the individual motor controller doesn't need to "know" where it's going in a planning sense. It just executes: "target position is X, current position is Y, apply correction." The question is how often that target gets updated. If the motor group only sends new targets once per second, the motor controller still runs at 1kHz doing PID on that static target. That works fine for smooth motion. The issue is when the TARGET should change mid-second because the trajectory planner sees something new. So you're right - the motor level can run at whatever frequency it wants for stability, but the TARGET update rate is what matters for reactivity. I conflated two things. Approach 2 robustness argument: If you plan a 1-second trajectory and execute it open-loop, and at 0.3 seconds the object you're reaching for shifts 2cm, you reach the wrong spot. If you replan at 30Hz, you see the shift at 0.33 seconds and your next trajectory chunk corrects. That's the robustness. It's not about motor stability, it's about responding to environmental changes faster than your trajectory chunk length. Phone compute - let me actually do the math: Pixel 6 has a Tensor G1 chip. Neural inference benchmarks: roughly 2-4 TOPS for the TPU, maybe 0.5 TOPS for CPU. A 100M parameter model at FP16 needs roughly 200M multiply-accumulate operations per inference. At 2 TOPS, that's 100ms per inference, so 10Hz max. For the trajectory planner running once per second, that's fine. For motor group at 30-100Hz, that's too slow. But here's the real issue: Android is not a real-time OS. Even if the chip is fast enough, the OS can pause your app for 50-100ms randomly for garbage collection, notifications, or background services. For the narrator and trajectory planner where 100ms jitter doesn't matter, phone works. For motor group where you need consistent 10-30ms timing, phone fails unpredictably. So: Phone CAN run narrator and trajectory planner. Phone CANNOT reliably run motor group timing. You still need something with real-time guarantees for the lower levels, which means microcontroller (ESP32/STM32) for the actual motor control loops. LeRobot usage: You don't NEED LeRobot. It's a convenience. It gives you tested implementations of ACT, Diffusion Policy, data collection scripts. You could build all that yourself. The question is whether building it yourself teaches you something valuable or just burns time. For your first arm, I'd use LeRobot to get something working, then replace pieces as you understand them. Motion capture for spider: Not external camera for the spider itself. The motion capture rig is for YOU, the human trainer. You wear IMUs, demonstrate walking motions, that data trains the spider's gait policy. The spider doesn't need cameras at all for basic locomotion - it uses proprioception (joint angles) and maybe an IMU on its body for balance. Cameras only matter if you want the spider to navigate visually. Kinematic fidelity measurement: Yes, autonomous measurement is possible. You command a trajectory, record actual joint positions via encoders, compare to commanded positions. The RMS error between commanded and actual is your kinematic fidelity. You can log this continuously during operation. What should coder do right now: Three concrete options: Spec the phone-based narrator + trajectory system: Define the API between phone (running narrator + VLA) and microcontroller (running motor control). Prove the architecture works with the compute split you're proposing. Build the IMU motion capture rig spec: Bill of materials, wiring diagram, data format, how it connects to training pipeline. This is your first $100 purchase. Design the manufacturing box frame: Dimensions, arm mounting points, camera positions, conveyor/turntable options. CAD or at least detailed sketch with measurements. Which one moves you forward fastest?

turns.originalText: Let me address your questions directly. Vision input by layer: You're right. Narrator and Task Decomposer need environment awareness (overhead camera). Trajectory Planner needs close manipulation view (wrist camera). Motor Group and below don't need vision at all, just proprioception (joint angles, motor current). Phone camera as environment camera: Yes, but the phone would need to be mounted overhead looking down, not held or on the wrist. If the phone IS the compute platform, you'd need a separate USB camera for overhead view while the phone is mounted somewhere accessible. Or: phone handles compute only, two separate cameras (overhead + wrist) feed into it via USB. RTOS alternatives to phone: The reason phone seems attractive: high compute, built-in sensors, cheap used. The problems: locked bootloader, Android-specific drivers, battery/power management complexity, no GPIO for motor control. Better options at similar price points: | Device | Price | Compute | RTOS Support | GPIO | Camera | |--------|-------|---------|--------------|------|--------| | Pixel 6 (rooted) | $150 used | 2-4 TOPS | Hacky at best | None | Yes | | Raspberry Pi 5 | $80 | 0.5 TOPS | Linux RT patch | 40 pins | USB cameras | | Orange Pi 5 | $90 | 6 TOPS (NPU) | Linux RT | 26 pins | USB cameras | | Jetson Orin Nano | $500 | 40 TOPS | Full RTOS | 40 pins | USB/CSI cameras | | ESP32-S3 + phone | $10 + $150 | Phone for NN, ESP for control | FreeRTOS on ESP | 34 pins | Phone camera | The Orange Pi 5 is interesting. RK3588S chip has a 6 TOPS NPU specifically for neural inference. $90. GPIO for motor control. Runs Linux with RT patches. You could put everything (layers 3-6) on one board with proper timing guarantees. Add two USB cameras ($30 each). Total compute platform: $150. ESP32 specifics: ESP32-S3: ~$10. Has 34 GPIO pins. Each servo needs 1 PWM pin. A 6-DOF arm needs 6 pins. Four arms would need 24 pins. You have headroom. The ESP32 can drive all motors for a 4-arm cell from one board. Communication: ESP32 has WiFi and Bluetooth built in. Phone sends trajectory data over WiFi, ESP32 interpolates and drives motors. Latency over local WiFi: 5-20ms typical. Acceptable for 1Hz trajectory updates. The limitation isn't pins, it's that ESP32 can't run neural nets at any useful speed. It's purely for motor control execution and anomaly detection (classical thresholds, not neural). LeRobot clarification: LeRobot is a training framework, not a runtime. You use it to: Collect demonstration data (records camera + joint positions during teleoperation) Train a policy (takes recorded data, outputs neural network weights) Export trained weights Then you take those weights and run inference wherever you want, phone, Orange Pi, Jetson, whatever. LeRobot doesn't run on the robot during operation. It's a development tool. What LeRobot gives you: tested training code so you don't debug gradient flow and data loading. What it doesn't give you: runtime inference code, communication protocols, motor control, any of the deployment stack. You could skip LeRobot entirely and write training code in PyTorch yourself. LeRobot just saves maybe 40 hours of debugging training pipelines. Given your answers: Experience: Solid foundation, can learn fast with AI assistance Budget: Up to $10K if proven useful, which means we can do this properly Fabrication: 3D printer access, can buy tools as needed Revised recommendation: Don't use the phone. Use Orange Pi 5 ($90) as your main compute. Two USB cameras (overhead + wrist). Direct PWM to servos. No ESP32 needed for first prototype. What coder should do: Design the Orange Pi 5 based single-arm control system. Good context drop. The haptic research I just did strengthens several points in that synthesis.
Key updates:
The GELLO force extension numbers are now concrete: 62%→93% on drawer opening, and the implementation uses DYNAMIXEL current control to reflect external torque estimates—no additional F/T sensors needed. That's your sub-$500 bilateral system right there.
DexForce's 76% vs 0% result is the strongest argument for why your motion capture suit needs force feedback, not just position tracking. Position-only demonstrations literally cannot teach dexterous tasks like unscrewing nuts or opening AirPods cases. The force information isn't optional.
The Bi-ACT architecture validates your hierarchy: it predicts joint angles, velocities, AND forces. Including force in both observations and action targets outperforms force-in-observation-only. Your motor group policies should output force targets, not just position targets, even if the low-level controller converts them to current commands.
What's new that matters for your stack:
Sensorless force estimation via disturbance observers enables bilateral control at the STM32 level without wrist F/T sensors. ROBOTIS OpenMANIPULATOR-X does this at 1kHz using accurate dynamics models. Your hybrid neural-PID joint controllers could estimate external force as a byproduct of the neural feedforward—same computation, free force feedback.
CMU's FACTR system achieved 64.7% improvement using "force-attending curriculum training"—start with easy force-insensitive tasks, gradually introduce contact-rich tasks. That's your training progression strategy.
Of those three research directions you listed, #2 (low-cost bilateral teleoperation under $1000) is now mostly answered. Want me to hit #1 (sim-to-real for hybrid neural-PID) or #3 (hexapod/octopod platforms with modular neural control)?

That's a solid capture of where we landed. The stack makes sense - the hierarchy matches what Figure, Physical Intelligence, and NVIDIA are doing, just decomposed for your hardware constraints and multi-arm scenario.
Looking at those three research directions:
Sim-to-real for hybrid neural-PID is probably your highest-leverage next step. You need this before anything runs on real hardware. The domain randomization question is particularly relevant because motor-level variations (friction, backlash, thermal drift) are exactly what the neural feedforward is supposed to learn - if you randomize them too aggressively in sim, the neural component learns nothing useful. Too little and it doesn't transfer.
Low-cost bilateral teleoperation is your data bottleneck. Without good demonstration data, nothing else matters. GELLO at ~$300 with the force feedback extension is compelling. DOGlove if you want finger dexterity later. SlimeVR-based is cheapest but loses the force feedback that gave that 11% boost.
Hexapod/octopod is interesting but feels like a distraction from the manufacturing cell unless you're genuinely pivoting to locomotion platforms.
My read: you need the teleoperation rig first because you can't train anything without data. Then sim-to-real because you need to validate the motor-level neural controllers before trusting them with real actuators. The spider stuff is cool but orthogonal to your 4-arm cell.
Want me to go deep on the bilateral teleoperation comparison? That feels like the immediate blocker - you can't collect demonstrations without the hardware, and the haptic feedback quality directly impacts policy performance.

turns.originalText: The wireless argument is compelling. Let me think through both options honestly. Phone + ESP32 wireless vs Orange Pi 5 wired: | Factor | Phone + ESP32 (wireless) | Orange Pi 5 (wired) | |--------|-------------------------|---------------------| | Wiring complexity | Minimal - just power to ESP32s, servos | Significant - GPIO runs to all servos | | Latency | 10-50ms WiFi/BT | <1ms direct GPIO | | Reliability | WiFi can drop, BT can desync | Rock solid | | Debugging | Harder - two devices | Easier - one device | | Camera flexibility | Phone camera + USB | USB only | | Cost | $150 phone + $40 (4x ESP32) = $190 | $90 + $60 cameras = $150 | | Portability | Phone is reusable for other projects | Dedicated hardware | The latency difference matters less than I initially suggested because you're running trajectory updates at 1Hz. 50ms jitter on a 1000ms cycle is 5%. The ESP32 handles the 1kHz PID loop locally with hard real-time guarantees regardless of phone latency. Bluetooth vs WiFi: Bluetooth (BLE): Lower power, simpler pairing, but limited bandwidth (~2 Mbps practical). For sending 100 joint position targets per second per arm, you need maybe 10KB/s per arm. Four arms = 40KB/s. BLE can handle this but with less headroom. WiFi: Higher bandwidth (50+ Mbps), lower latency (5-10ms vs 20-50ms BLE), but more power hungry and slightly more complex setup. For your use case, WiFi is better. The ESP32 stays powered from the frame anyway, and you want the lower latency for anomaly feedback. The phone architecture wins for prototyping because: Zero wire runs between compute and actuators Phone camera works as overhead view if mounted correctly You can iterate on the neural net side by just updating the phone app ESP32s are $10 each and handle all timing-critical stuff locally If a phone dies, you swap in another phone, not rewire a custom board What you actually need to buy: | Item | Quantity | Unit Cost | Total | |------|----------|-----------|-------| | Used Pixel 6 or similar | 1 | $150 | $150 | | ESP32-S3 DevKit | 4 | $10 | $40 | | USB-C hub (for wrist cameras) | 1 | $20 | $20 | | USB cameras (wrist mount) | 4 | $15 | $60 | | Phone mount (overhead) | 1 | $20 | $20 | | Compute total | | | $290 | Then arms and frame on top of that. LeRobot for training: You collect demonstrations on the real hardware. LeRobot records camera frames + joint positions + timestamps. You run training on your desktop/laptop GPU (or cloud). LeRobot outputs a trained model file. You load that model onto the phone for inference. The phone never trains, just runs inference on the trained weights. Training is not real-time. You collect data, then train overnight, then deploy. The real-time part is just data collection (teleoperation) and inference (running the trained policy). What coder should build: The phone app architecture. Specifically: Camera input handling (overhead phone camera + USB wrist cameras) Neural net inference runtime (ONNX or TFLite for the VLA) WiFi protocol to ESP32s (trajectory packets, anomaly responses) Cloud API integration for narrator/decomposer Data logging for LeRobot-compatible training data collection This is the core of your system. Everything else is mechanical assembly and training. Want me to send this spec to coder?
